title: Design a Load Balancer
tagline: Spread traffic over many servers, drop the ones that fail, and never become the failure yourself.

statement.prompt: Design a **load balancer** that sits in front of a fleet of web servers and distributes incoming requests across them.
context: You are in a 45-minute interview. Many candidates answer "use round robin". Interviewers want to see the whole picture.
The service is public and traffic varies through the day.
Think of the managed balancers in AWS (ALB and NLB) or software like Nginx and HAProxy.
given: About **50 million requests a day**, peaking at **3 times** the average.
Each backend server handles about **500 requests per second**.
Servers are added and removed during deployments and scaling.
Requests vary from a few milliseconds to several seconds.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of them.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working version on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are health checking, choosing an algorithm for uneven traffic and removing the balancer as a single point of failure.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

scope_in: Making the balancer itself highly available
great: Compares **Layer 4 and Layer 7** and picks one with a reason.
Chooses an algorithm that matches the request pattern.
Designs health checks with thresholds and connection draining.
Makes the balancer redundant across zones.

concepts.def: L4 forwards TCP/UDP by IP and port (fast). L7 understands HTTP, so it can route by path, header or cookie, and terminate TLS.
A regular test (such as GET /health) used to decide whether a server should get traffic.
When removing a server, stop new requests but let in-flight ones finish.
Many locations announce the same IP; the network sends each user to the nearest one.
Sending a user to the same server every time. Convenient, but it makes servers stateful.

numbers: Servers needed = peak rate / per-server capacity, plus spares
A single good balancer handles **tens of thousands** of requests per second

takeaways: Use a **Layer 7 balancer** for path routing and TLS, with L4 in front at very large scale.
Pick **least connections** for uneven requests, **weighted** for mixed servers.
**Health checks with thresholds** and **connection draining** keep users safe during failures.
Keep servers **stateless** and run the balancer as a **redundant pair across zones**.

tradeoffs.cost: More latency and CPU than Layer 4

extensions: Rate limiting and DDoS protection at the edge
Global load balancing across regions with DNS

steps.title: What must a load balancer do?
steps.prompt: You are asked to design a load balancer. Which belong in the **core** scope?
steps.hint: Think of a traffic policeman: he directs cars, he does not drive them.
steps.explain: Core: **distribute, health-check, add/remove servers, pluggable algorithm**. TLS termination and sticky sessions are good extras.

notes: Core: distribute requests, health checks, add/remove servers, pluggable algorithm

options.text: Choose a server using a configurable algorithm
options.why: Round robin, least connections and so on.

options.text: Add and remove servers without dropping traffic
options.why: Scaling and deployments need this.

options.text: Accept client connections and forward each request to one backend server
options.why: The defining job.

options.text: Run the application business logic
options.why: The balancer routes. It does not know your product.

options.text: Store user data durably
options.why: A balancer is stateless apart from small bits of configuration.

options.text: Detect unhealthy servers and stop sending them traffic
options.why: Without health checks it just spreads failures around.

steps.title: What qualities matter?
steps.prompt: Pick the qualities a load balancer must have.
steps.hint: What happens to the whole site if this box is slow or dead?
steps.explain: A balancer is **in the path of every request**, so be paranoid about **latency** and **availability**.

notes: Qualities: negligible latency, no single point of failure, scales to very many connections

options.text: Very high availability, no single point of failure
options.why: If the balancer dies, everything behind it is unreachable.

options.text: Horizontal scalability for hundreds of thousands of connections
options.why: It sits in front of the whole fleet.

options.text: Rich query capabilities
options.why: Not its job.

options.text: Extra latency of well under a millisecond or two
options.why: Every request goes through it.

options.text: Strong consistency of data with transactions
options.why: No data of its own to keep consistent.

steps.title: How big must it be?
steps.prompt: The site serves **50 million requests a day**. Each server comfortably handles **500 requests per second**. Peak is **3 times** the average. How many **servers** are needed at peak (round up)?
steps.hint: Average per second first, then multiply for peak, then divide by server capacity.
steps.explain: **4 servers plus spares** shows the point: one balancer handles this easily (a good one handles tens of thousands per second); the server fleet is what grows.

notes: Scale example: about 600 req/s average, 1,800 peak, so 4-6 backend servers

work: 1,740 / 500 = 3.5, so **4 servers** (add 1 or 2 more as spare capacity)

steps.title: Layer 4 or Layer 7?
steps.prompt: Your product has `/api` servers and `/images` servers and needs TLS termination. Which type of load balancer do you need?
steps.hint: Does the decision need to look inside the HTTP request?
steps.explain: **L4 = fast and simple, L7 = smart.** Large systems often use L4 in front of L7.

notes: Type: Layer 7 balancer (path routing, TLS termination); L4 in front at very high scale

steps.followup: When would you pick Layer 4 instead?

options.text: DNS round robin only
options.why: No health checks and caches linger, so a dead server keeps receiving traffic.

options.text: Layer 7 (HTTP aware)
options.why: Only L7 can read the URL path and decide `/api` vs `/images`, and terminate TLS.

options.text: No load balancer: clients choose a server
options.why: Pushes failure handling to every client.

options.text: Layer 4 (TCP only)
options.why: L4 sees IPs and ports only, so it cannot route by path. It is faster and good for plain TCP such as databases.

steps.title: What are the main components?
steps.prompt: Which components make up the design?
steps.explain: Draw **clients -> balancer pair -> servers**, with the **health checker** feeding the pool. Then explain each.

notes: Components: balancer pair, server pool, health checker, heartbeat between the pair

options.text: A standby balancer with a heartbeat for failover
options.why: Removes the single point of failure.

options.text: A health checker that tests each server
options.why: Drives which servers are in the pool.

options.text: A pool of backend servers
options.why: What we are balancing.

options.text: The load balancer (a proxy that picks a server per request)
options.why: The core.

options.text: A relational database holding every request
options.why: Adds latency and a bottleneck for no reason.

steps.title: Which algorithm?
steps.prompt: Requests vary hugely in cost: some take 5 ms, some take 5 seconds (file exports). Servers are identical. Which algorithm balances best?
steps.explain: **Round robin** for equal, short requests. **Least connections** when durations differ. **Weighted** for different server sizes. **Consistent hash** for cache affinity. **Power of two choices** is a cheap, strong default at scale.

notes: Algorithm: least connections (weighted if servers differ), configurable

steps.followup: Why does picking two random servers and taking the less busy work nearly as well as checking all of them?

options.text: IP hash
options.why: Keeps a client on one server, which is good for caches but unbalanced if a few clients are heavy.

options.text: Always the first server
options.why: Not balancing at all.

options.text: Least connections
options.why: Sends new work to the server with the fewest in-flight requests, so a server stuck on slow requests is avoided.

options.text: Plain round robin
options.why: Gives each server the same count of requests, not the same load. A server can pile up slow ones.

steps.title: Health checking
steps.prompt: A server starts failing. Put these events in the order a good design handles them.
steps.explain: Use **thresholds both ways** (N failures to remove, M successes to add) and **connection draining**. Combine **active** checks with **passive** ones (watching real 5xx errors).

notes: Health: active /health checks, N failures to remove, M successes to re-add, connection draining, passive 5xx detection

items.text: The health checker's `GET /health` to the server times out
items.why: Active checks find problems even without traffic.

items.text: After 3 failed checks in a row the server is marked unhealthy
items.why: Several failures, not one, avoids reacting to a blip (flapping).

items.text: The balancer stops choosing it; in-flight requests finish (draining)
items.why: No new traffic, no cut-off users.

items.text: Checks continue; after 2 successes the server returns to the pool
items.why: Needs consecutive successes to avoid bouncing in and out.

items.text: An alert fires if too many servers are unhealthy at once
items.why: A mass failure is a bigger problem than one box.

steps.title: Sessions and sticky routing
steps.prompt: Users stay logged in. Where should session data live so any server can serve any request?
steps.hint: What happens to pinned users when their server dies?
steps.explain: **Stateless servers + shared session store** beat sticky sessions. Use stickiness only as a small optimisation (for example a warm local cache).

notes: Sessions: stateless servers, session data in a shared store; stickiness optional

options.text: In the load balancer's memory
options.why: Makes the balancer stateful and fragile.

options.text: In each server's memory, with the balancer pinning each user to one server
options.why: Works until that server dies or you scale down; load becomes uneven.

options.text: In a shared store (Redis or a database), so servers stay stateless
options.why: Any server can handle any user; scaling down or crashing loses nothing.

options.text: In a cookie containing the user's raw password
options.why: Never.

steps.title: Remove the single point of failure
steps.prompt: Which techniques keep the balancer itself available?
steps.hint: Two of everything, in different places.
steps.explain: Same rule as for every layer: **redundancy across zones**. In the cloud, a managed balancer (ALB/NLB) does this for you, but explain *how* it works.

notes: HA: balancer pair (active-passive or active-active), multi-zone, heartbeat failover

options.text: Spread them across availability zones
options.why: A whole zone can fail.

options.text: Let clients retry forever until it recovers
options.why: A retry storm makes it worse.

options.text: An active-passive pair sharing a floating IP, with a heartbeat
options.why: The standby takes over the IP when the heartbeat stops.

options.text: Run a single very powerful balancer
options.why: Still a single point of failure.

options.text: Or active-active balancers behind DNS or anycast
options.why: Uses both nodes and survives a loss.

steps.title: When one balancer is not enough
steps.prompt: Traffic grows to millions of connections. What are sensible next steps?
steps.explain: Tiered balancing: **DNS/anycast -> L4 -> L7 -> servers**. Each tier is scaled horizontally and stays stateless.

notes: At huge scale: DNS/anycast -> L4 tier -> L7 tier -> servers

options.text: Put L4 balancers (ECMP or anycast) in front of a tier of L7 balancers
options.why: Spreads connection load, then smart routing.

options.text: Use a bigger single machine forever
options.why: Hits a ceiling.

options.text: Remove health checks to save time
options.why: Saves nothing and sends users to dead servers.

options.text: Offload TLS to dedicated hardware or the edge
options.why: TLS handshakes are CPU heavy.

options.text: Scale L7 balancers horizontally and keep them stateless
options.why: Add boxes for more throughput.

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: In two or three sentences: what are the trade-offs of a Layer 7 balancer with least-connections routing?
steps.hint: What does every request pay for the smarts?
steps.explain: Always name **who pays** for a choice: latency, cost, complexity or consistency.

notes: Trade-offs: L7 flexibility vs latency, redundancy vs idle capacity

steps.model: A Layer 7 balancer gives **smart routing and TLS termination** but adds a little **latency and CPU cost** compared with Layer 4 and needs more capacity. Least connections adapts to uneven requests but needs the balancer to **track state** per server. A balancer pair removes the single point of failure at the cost of **idle capacity and failover complexity**. If traffic or latency demanded it I would put an L4 tier in front.
points: Routing intelligence vs added latency/cost (L7 vs L4)
Said when to change (L4 tier at huge scale)
